article_hormones_intro: Hormone levels shift continuously across your cycle. Those shifts affect more than bleeding — they touch your energy, your sleep and your mood. Knowing what happens in each phase makes the ups and downs easier to make sense of.
article_hormones_b1: A cycle runs from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. For most people it is around 28 days, but anywhere from 21 to 35 days is common and normal. Bleeding usually lasts 2 to 7 days, about 5 on average, and tends to be heaviest on the first two days.
article_hormones_b2: When estrogen and progesterone drop to their lowest, the uterine lining sheds — that is your period. As bleeding ends, estrogen starts climbing again and the lining rebuilds. Energy and focus often pick up during this stretch.
article_hormones_b3: LH, released by your brain, tells the ovary to release an egg. It surges about 36 hours before ovulation and peaks around 12 hours before. Ovulation usually falls 12 to 16 days before your next period starts. Because sperm can survive up to 7 days, the fertile window is wider than ovulation day alone.
article_hormones_h4: Luteal phase and when to see a doctor
article_hormones_b4:
After ovulation, progesterone rises and prepares the lining for a possible pregnancy. If there is no pregnancy, hormones fall again and the cycle restarts.

It is worth seeing a clinician if your cycle is regularly shorter than 24 days or longer than 38, if it changes suddenly, or if your bleeding is very heavy.
article_pms_intro: Premenstrual symptoms are common: more than 90% of women report some. They usually appear in the five days before a period and ease within four days after bleeding starts.
article_pms_b1: The evidence clusters around a few nutrients. Calcium may reduce fatigue, cravings and low mood. Vitamin B6 may help with moodiness, irritability, bloating and anxiety. Magnesium may ease migraine-type headaches. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (1–2 grams a day) may reduce cramps and other symptoms.
article_pms_b2: Regular aerobic exercise throughout the month, about eight hours of sleep a night, and stress-lowering practices such as yoga, massage or meditation are all recommended. Cutting back on caffeine, salt and sugar in the two weeks before your period is another suggested step. Smaller, more frequent meals help some people.
article_pms_b3: See a clinician if lifestyle changes have not helped or your symptoms are affecting daily life. It is also worth asking before starting supplements: this page is general information, not personal medical advice.
article_partner_intro: Talking to your partner about your cycle is not complaining — it is sharing the map of something you both live with. When they know what to expect, there is less misreading, and less of a burden on you to explain it from scratch every time.
article_partner_b1: Premenstrual symptoms typically start in the five days before bleeding and ease within four days after it begins. Sharing that shows a mood shift is a known pattern, not a personal stance. Partner sharing in the app exists for exactly this: they can see which phase you are in.
article_partner_b2: "Be understanding" stays abstract. "Let us not make evening plans this week", "could you bring me a hot water bottle", "I want to be alone today and I am not angry with you" — concrete sentences let the other person know what to actually do.
article_partner_b3: A conversation opened at peak symptoms turns into an argument easily. Talking on a comfortable day in your cycle makes it easier for both of you to listen without getting defensive. Noting together what worked saves you from having the same conversation next cycle.
article_mood_intro: Mood changes before a period are common and real. Health services say the cause is not fully understood, and that it is likely tied to shifting hormone levels across the cycle — with some people affected more than others.
article_mood_b1: Mood swings, feeling low or irritable, anxiety and tearfulness are frequently reported. They can come alongside tiredness, trouble sleeping, bloating, breast tenderness, headaches and appetite changes.
article_mood_b2:
Regular exercise, a balanced diet, enough sleep and stress-lowering practices like yoga or meditation are recommended. Avoiding smoking and heavy drinking is on the list too.

Logging your symptoms across a few cycles pays off: seeing the pattern helps you plan, and gives you something concrete to show a clinician.
article_mood_b3:
See a clinician if symptoms are affecting your daily life or lifestyle changes are not enough. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a separate, more severe condition that can bring intense anxiety, anger or depression.

If you are having thoughts of harming yourself or of suicide, do not carry that alone — reach emergency services or someone close to you without delay.
article_iron_intro: Heavy periods are one of the most common causes of iron deficiency anaemia. Without enough iron, your blood cannot carry oxygen well, and that usually shows up first as tiredness.
article_iron_b1: The most common are tiredness, shortness of breath, heart palpitations, pale skin and headaches. Less commonly: ringing in the ears, a changed sense of taste, mouth ulcers, a sore tongue, hair loss, spoon-shaped nails and restless legs syndrome.
article_iron_b2:
Iron-rich foods include dark-green leafy vegetables such as watercress and curly kale, fortified cereals and bread, meat, dried fruit such as apricots, prunes and raisins, and beans, peas and lentils.

Iron from plants absorbs better alongside vitamin C, so adding orange, peppers or tomato to a meal helps. Tea, coffee, dairy and foods high in phytic acid make iron harder to absorb, so they are best kept away from the meal itself.
article_iron_b3: If you have these signs, see a clinician: iron deficiency shows up on a simple blood test, and it is worth checking whether something other than bleeding is behind it. Do not start iron supplements without medical advice — iron you do not need can be harmful.
article_disclaimer: This is general information, not personal medical advice. If something worries you, speak to a health professional.
